prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of uncertainty and many-body regimes

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B008 alone, Katori and Ye. Round 1 sharpened the case rather than weakening it. The new physical principle, which Mehlig asked for, is the magic wavelength: choosing the lattice wavelength so that the light shift is equal for the two clock levels removes the trap perturbation to first order, and Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil shifts. That lets very many neutral atoms be interrogated at once without giving up accuracy, so the statistical limit falls by orders of magnitude while the systematic limit stays controlled. This is a different idea from the comb, which is a ruler for optical frequencies, and from single-ion control, which works with one quantum system. The idea has been demonstrated, reproduced and surpassed in Sr, Yb and Hg systems, and it has already produced observations that were not possible before: gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, spin-exchange and many-body effects visible in the clock line, and routine intercontinental comparisons. Five members prefer it, and Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson each accept it as a fallback or alternative, so it is also the outcome the committee as a whole can defend. The credit boundary is a judgement but a defensible one: Katori for the concept and first lattice clock, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and stability and for the many-body physics.
statement.case_against: The objections that remain are real. Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig weigh a discovery about nature above a measurement capability, and no deviation from standard physics has yet been seen with lattice clocks, so part of the case rests on opened observables rather than new phenomena. The comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes sit next to this lineage and some in the Academy will read the clock as a refinement. The SI second has not been redefined. Other groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, Gill, Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr) made real contributions, and in my own field I know the atomic-structure inputs to the systematic budgets came from many hands, so a two-name credit is a boundary drawn with judgement, not a statement that no one else mattered. Finally my own proximity to the field could bias me toward valuing it.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether the lattice clock's novelty is a new physical principle or a very large improvement of an established technology, and says he wants this argued from the atomic-physics side.
responses.response: It is a new principle, and I can say why in plain terms. In a trapped-atom clock the trap light normally shifts the two clock levels by different amounts, so the better you hold the atoms the more you disturb the very transition you want to measure. Katori's insight was that there is a wavelength at which the two levels shift identically, so the trap becomes invisible to the clock line, while the tight confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects. That is what allows millions of atoms to be used at once, and it is why the quantum projection noise limit that constrains single-ion clocks can be beaten in stability. It is not a smaller version of a known technique. I would add that this principle also made the many-body physics reachable, which Ye's group exploited. I accept that this does not make it a particle or a state of matter, and I understand why you weigh that differently.

responses.point: Danielsson accepts that B008 has the cleanest attribution but argues the Higgs discovery is a larger result, and that clean attribution should not by itself outweigh size.
responses.response: I agree that attribution alone should not decide the prize, and I would not argue it that way. The Higgs is a larger result in the sense you mean, and I defer to you on the particle-physics record. My difficulty is the one you concede yourself: the trio from four credited founders is a judgement the record cannot settle, and dropping Della Negra or Virdee or Jenni changes the story. For me the deciding factor is not that B008 is easy to credit but that it is a complete, reproduced, understood result where the credit boundary matches identifiable steps. I also do not think the clock merely extends the 2005 and 2012 prizes. If the committee finds a rule for ATLAS and CMS that it trusts, I would not oppose B056, and I would keep it as my second alternative.

responses.point: Kroll adds that the 10^-18 claims rest on a handful of systematics controlled differently in the JILA and RIKEN/Tokyo systems, and discloses his year in Hall's laboratory with a possible connection to Ye.
responses.response: I agree with his laboratory point, and it answers the chair's question about independence. The main systematics (blackbody radiation shift, lattice light shift including hyperpolarisability, density shifts) have been studied by several groups, with essential contributions from theory and measurement outside Katori and Ye, for example the SYRTE and PTB work and the atomic-structure calculations that constrain blackbody and polarisability corrections. As I recall it, those contributions refined the budgets rather than establishing the lattice-clock concept or the first demonstration of the regime, and the agreement of independent systems is what makes the claim robust. That supports the invention-plus-leading-realisation boundary, but I should say that I am working from recollection of the literature, and I would welcome a check. On recusal, I think his tie is a year in a neighbouring laboratory with no collaboration with Ye, so full recusal seems unnecessary; I would suggest he participates with the disclosure noted, as he has offered.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators as a new state of matter over an inventive measurement tool, and asks whether the SI redefinition of the second is better waited for.
responses.response: I would not wait, and I would say this plainly: the prize is for a demonstrated capability and a stable physical result, and tying it to a metrology decision would be tying it to something we do not control. On the substance, I accept that a new state of matter is a strong kind of discovery, and for me B049 is a serious candidate. But the credit problem you describe is not a minor drafting issue: the HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, not the Kane-Mele graphene model, and a three-name cap cannot hold both the 2D and 3D stories. A citation that misstates the lineage would be worse than no prize on that topic. I rank B049 as my first alternative, and I would support it if Mehlig and you can settle a citation that is honest about the lineage.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues accept the magic-wavelength lattice with many neutral atoms as a distinct principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or still read it as a refinement.

Whether the credit boundary of Katori and Ye is fair against SYRTE, PTB, NIST and the ion-clock lineage; my account of who established which systematic comes from my reading of the literature and should be checked against the record.

Whether the absence of any detected deviation from standard physics should weigh against a fundamental-physics prize; I think demonstrated results (millimetre redshift, many-body clock physics) are enough, but this is a judgement.
For B049 and B056 I defer to colleagues in condensed-matter and particle physics on whether a defensible attribution exists.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and Keller attosecond groups, which is field proximity for atomic, molecular and optical candidates. I have no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or their laboratories, and no ties to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee or Della Negra, so I see no recusal requirement for B008. As someone who has done systematic-shift and atomic-structure calculations of the kind that enter clock budgets, I am an informed reader of this field, which the committee should weigh as expertise but also as possible bias.
